analysis.investment_thesis: Equitas Small Finance Bank's revenue grows at a modest 17.4% CAGR, but an 82% collapse in net profit (INR 799 Cr → INR 147 Cr in FY2025) driven by runaway finance costs signals a structural deterioration that disqualifies it as a Fisher-style growth company. Until management demonstrates control over asset quality and restores earnings trajectory, this is not a business worth owning at any price.
key_strengths: Diversified lending franchise across microfinance, vehicles, housing, and gold loans gives multiple growth avenues
Total assets nearly doubled in 3 years (INR 26,948 → 52,836 Cr) showing franchise expansion capacity
Strong DII ownership at 50.87% reflects domestic institutional conviction in the long-term SFB model
key_risks: Finance costs growing at 29.1% CAGR — far outpacing revenue growth of 17.4% — directly crushing profitability
Net profit collapsed 82% YoY (INR 799 Cr → 147 Cr) suggesting severe asset quality stress in the micro/MSME book
ROE of just 2.42% — abysmal for a bank and wholly incompatible with Fisher's >20% ROE requirement
red_flags: Earnings CAGR of -19.4% over 3 years while revenue grows — a widening scissors pattern
Finance cost (INR 3,060 Cr) now exceeds total revenue of FY2022 (INR 2,513 Cr) — interest burden is existential
Trailing P/E of 50.93x on near-zero earnings is misleading; forward P/E of 11.28x bakes in a recovery that is not yet visible in the data
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From a Scuttlebutt lens, Equitas SFB operates in structurally attractive segments — microfinance, used vehicle finance, affordable housing — where demand is genuine and underserved. Revenue has grown respectably at 17.4% CAGR, and the balance sheet has scaled aggressively. However, this is a tale of expansion without earnings discipline. Finance costs have ballooned from INR 1,421 Cr (2022) to INR 3,060 Cr (2025) at a 29.1% CAGR, nearly 10 percentage points faster than revenue — a pattern that signals either deposit repricing pressure, aggressive wholesale borrowing, or deteriorating loan mix. The result is an 82% profit crash in a single year, leaving ROE at a humiliating 2.42%.

Fisher's 15-point checklist demands that management demonstrate the ability to maintain and improve margins while growing. Equitas's management has failed this test badly: profit margins are collapsing even as the top line expands, suggesting either poor cost controls, worsening credit quality in the microfinance book (consistent with industry-wide stress in FY2025), or both. The forward P/E of 11.28x tells us the market is pricing in a sharp earnings rebound — but with no visible catalyst and operating leverage working against the bank, that recovery is speculative. This is not a great business at a cheap price; it is a troubled business at a fair price. I would require two consecutive quarters of NIM stabilization and profit recovery before revisiting.
